questions.label: Q1
questions.teaser: The painting shown is Hunters in the Snow by Pieter Bruegel the Elder , created in 1565 CE. The painting depicts human activity within a natural landscape. Select and completely identify another…
questions.promptText:
Art Resource, NY
1. The painting shown is Hunters in the Snow by Pieter Bruegel the Elder , created in 1565 CE. The
painting depicts human activity within a natural landscape.
Select and completely identify another painting that depicts human activity within a natural
landscape. You may select a painting from the list below or any other relevant painting.
Describe one visual characteristic of Hunters in the Snow and one visual characteristic of your
selected painting.
Using specific visual evidence from Hunters in the Snow and specific visual evidence from your
selected painting, explain ONE difference in how the artists depicted human activity in the
natural landscape.
Using specific visual evidence from Hunters in the Snow and specific visual evidence from your
selected painting, explain ANOTHER difference in how the artists depicted human activity in the
natural landscape.
Make a claim that explains one similarity or difference in why the artists depicted human
activity in the natural landscape.
Support your claim using specific contextual evidence from Hunters in the Snow and specific
contextual evidence from your selected painting.
When identifying the work you select, you should try to include all of the following identifiers:
title or designation, name of the artist and/or culture of origin, date of creation, and materials.
You will earn credit for the identification if you provide at least two accurate identifiers, but
you will not be penalized if any additional identifiers you provide are inaccurate. If you select
a work from the list below, you must include at least two accurate identifiers beyond those that
are given.
The Swing
Travelers among Mountains and Streams
The Court of Gayumars
questions.scoringGuide: AP Art History Q1, Long Essay Comparison, 8 points, each point earned independently. Task A (1): select and completely identify another work fitting the prompt (≥2 accurate identifiers beyond the given title — artist, date, materials, culture, or style). Task B (2): accurately describe ONE visual characteristic of the given work (Point 2) AND ONE of the selected work (Point 3). Task C (2): use visual evidence from BOTH works to explain ONE difference (Point 4) and ANOTHER difference (Point 5) in how the artists depicted the prompt's subject. Task D (3): articulate a claim about one similarity/difference in WHY the artists depicted it (Point 6), then support it with specific CONTEXTUAL evidence from the given work (Point 7) and from the selected work (Point 8). Describe = characteristics beyond naming; contextual evidence = about the work's culture/purpose/patronage, distinct from visual description.

rubric.name: Part A
rubric.criteria: Award 0–1 point for part A exactly as the official 2025 scoring guideline for this question specifies.

rubric.name: Part B
rubric.criteria: Award 0–2 points for part B exactly as the official 2025 scoring guideline for this question specifies.

rubric.name: Part C
rubric.criteria: Award 0–2 points for part C exactly as the official 2025 scoring guideline for this question specifies.

rubric.name: Part D
rubric.criteria: Award 0–3 points for part D exactly as the official 2025 scoring guideline for this question specifies.

examples.label: Sample 1A
examples.summary: Q1 Comparison scored 8/8 (all tasks A,B1,B2,C1,C2,D1,D2,D3). Selected Travelers among Mountains and Streams (identified culture 'Chinese' + material 'ink'). Described a visual characteristic of each work; explained two differences (relative size/importance of figures vs. landscape; degree of human impact on the environment); made a claim tied to differing cultural understandings and supported it with contextual evidence from both (European 16th-c. use of nature's resources; Daoist view of humans as a small part of the world). Full-credit model.

examples.label: Sample 1B
examples.summary: Q1 scored 6/8 (A,B1,B2,C1,C2,D1 earned; D2,D3 = 0). Selected The Swing (identified 'France', 'oil paint on canvas'). Described a visual characteristic of each; explained two+ differences (winter activity vs. clandestine play; work vs. leisure/affluence). Made a claim (setting impacts lifestyle) but did NOT support it with specific CONTEXTUAL evidence from either work, forfeiting the two contextual points. Shows the common gap: strong visual analysis but missing the contextual support in Task D.

examples.label: Sample 1C
examples.summary: Q1 scored 4/8 (B1,B2,C1,C2 earned; A,D1,D2,D3 = 0). Did not attempt Task A (no identification of a comparison work) or Task D (no claim + contextual evidence). Still earned both description points and both difference-explanation points (mood of loss vs. illicit secrecy; reactions to cold vs. warm weather — a minor inaccuracy did not negate an otherwise accurate explanation). Illustrates that the visual tasks (B, C) are independently earnable even when A and D are skipped.

questions.label: Q2
questions.teaser: Contemporary artists often use installations to communicate political, cultural, or personal meaning. Select and completely identify one work of art from the list below or any other relevant work…
questions.promptText:
Note: There are no images provided for Question 2.
2. Contemporary artists often use installations to communicate political, cultural, or personal
meaning.
Select and completely identify one work of art from the list below or any other relevant work
from the Global Contemporary (1980 CE to Present) in which the artist uses an installation to
communicate political, cultural, or personal meaning.
Explain how the installation communicates political, cultural, or personal meaning.
In your response, you should do the following:
• Provide two accurate identifiers for the work of art you have selected.
• Respond to the prompt with an art historically defensible claim or thesis that establishes
a line of reasoning.
• Support your claim with at least two examples of relevant visual and/or contextual
evidence.
• Explain how the evidence supports the claim.
• Corroborate or qualify your claim by explaining relevant connections, providing nuance,
or considering diverse views.
When identifying the work you select, you should try to include all of the following identifiers:
title or designation, artist, culture of origin, date of creation, and materials. You will earn
credit for the identification if you provide at least two accurate identifiers, but you will not be
penalized if any additional identifiers you provide are inaccurate. If you select a work from the
list below, you must include at least two accurate identifiers beyond those that are given.
Shibboleth
En la Barberia no se Llora (No Crying Allowed in the Barbershop)
Kui Hua Zi (Sunflower Seeds)
questions.scoringGuide: AP Art History Q2, Long Essay Visual/Contextual Analysis, 6 points, each earned independently. Task A (1): provide two accurate identifiers for the selected work. Task B (1): respond with an art-historically defensible claim/thesis. Task C (2): support the claim with at least two examples of relevant visual and/or contextual evidence. Task D (1): explain how the evidence supports the claim. Task E (1): corroborate or qualify the claim by explaining relevant connections. Points are independent — a response can earn evidence points without the claim point, etc.

examples.label: Sample 2A
examples.summary: Q2 Visual/Contextual Analysis scored 6/6 — earns all tasks: two accurate identifiers, a defensible claim, at least two examples of relevant visual/contextual evidence, an explanation of how the evidence supports the claim, and a corroborating/qualifying connection. questions.promptText:

The work shown is The Valley of Mexico (El Valle de México) by Jose María Velasco, created in
1888 CE. This work is not from the required image set.
3. In your response you should do the following:
Describe two visual characteristics of The Valley of Mexico (El Valle de México).

questions.scoringGuide: AP Art History Q3, Visual Analysis, 5 points (Tasks A–E, 1 point each, independent). A: accurately describe ONE visual characteristic of the shown work. B: accurately describe ANOTHER visual characteristic. C: use specific visual evidence to explain how the artist creates a particular effect (e.g. a sense of space/depth). D: use specific visual evidence to explain how the artist guides the viewer. E: use specific visual or contextual evidence to explain a further point about the work. Describe = characteristics beyond naming; the explain tasks require specific visual evidence tied to the effect.

questions.label: Q5
questions.teaser: In your response you should do the following: Correctly attribute the work shown to the specific culture from the Indigenous Americas (1000 BCE–1980 CE) in which it was created. Using two examples…
questions.promptText:
© The Trustees of the British Museum
This work is not part of the required image set.
5. In your response you should do the following:
Correctly attribute the work shown to the specific culture from the Indigenous Americas (1000
BCE–1980 CE) in which it was created.
Using two examples of specific visual evidence, justify the attribution by describing relevant
similarities between the work shown and another work of the same type created by the same
culture.
Using two examples of specific visual and/or contextual evidence, explain how the work shown
may have reinforced the values or beliefs of the culture in which it was created.
questions.scoringGuide: AP Art History Q5, Attribution, 5 points (Tasks A–E, 1 point each, independent). A: correctly attribute the shown work to its specific culture/tradition. B: justify the attribution by describing ONE relevant visual similarity to known works of that culture. C: justify with ANOTHER relevant visual similarity. D: explain ONE way the work may have reinforced the values or beliefs of its culture. E: explain ANOTHER such way. The justification tasks require visual similarities to the attributed culture; the value tasks require explained cultural significance.
